title: Watcher, ladder, routing and backstop
bridge: The progress watcher is like a code reviewer watching your terminal over your shoulder. Except it never says "you took too long". It only notices when you repeat yourself. Then it steps in one rung at a time: a hint, a re-plan, more thought, a fresh start, a person.
intro: We never limit an agent's time, turns or budget. So we need another way to catch an agent going in circles. This lesson builds the watcher that measures real progress and the ladder that steps in. It adds the model routing the ladder climbs, and a far cost backstop that pauses only between turns.

picture.caption: Every tool result feeds the watcher; flat progress climbs the ladder; the backstop checks spend only at step boundaries.

steps.text: every tool result becomes a small event
progress resets flatFor; repeats name a loop
rungs 1-2 inside the turn: a nudge, then a re-plan
rungs 3-5 at the step boundary: think harder, fresh start
afterStep reads the run's spend; shadow mode only logs
rung 5 or a live backstop: ask in the thread, keep the session

sections.h: A flaky test and no time limit
p: Nova runs npx playwright test login.spec.ts. It times out. Nova runs it again, and again, with the same error. A time limit would kill the run at some hour and throw away the good work before the loop.

We measure progress, not activity. Real progress is a check that failed and now passes, a plan item done, or a file read for the first time. Activity without progress is a sign of a loop. A loop is a reason to change approach, not to kill the run.

Four pieces do this. The watcher keeps score. The ladder steps in. The routing table says which model and effort each job gets, and how to think harder. The backstop catches a runaway the watcher missed, far above a normal ticket's cost.

callout.text: No maxTurns, no maxBudgetUsd, no taskBudget, no time limit. Only a person's Stop ends a run that is still working.

sections.h: The watcher, part 1: every tool result
p: The watcher is a hook (lesson p8-4) registered for PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure, so it sees every tool result. WatchEvent.of turns the hook's input into a small record. Timestamps and temp paths are stripped, and numbers in errors are masked. So two runs of the same command look the same.
sections.because: We keep a score instead of a clock, because a slow but useful run must never look like a stuck one.

notes.text: The bundled harness imports the SDK from /core (lesson g3-1). HookCallback is the type of a hook function.
The last 200 events. Old ones fall off.
How often each error signature (the first error line, numbers masked) has appeared.
The hashes each file had after each edit, to spot undo and redo.
Checks that are failing right now, by command.
flatFor counts tool events since the last real progress.
The hook function. The SDK calls it after every tool call, failed or not.
One record: tool, input hash, output hash, error signature, and the file hash after an edit.
Progress resets the counter to 0; anything else adds 1.
The verdict goes into run state and the heartbeat. The ladder reads it.
Return nothing for now. The ladder (section 6) makes this return extra context.

sections.h: The watcher, part 2: progress and loops
p: progressed decides what counts as progress. loopKind names the loop, following the stuck detector in OpenHands, an open-source coding agent. Four kinds: same action and result 3 times, same error 3 times, a file back to an earlier state, and A-B-A-B.
sections.because: We name the kind of loop, because the nudge works better when it tells the model exactly what it keeps doing.

notes.text: A check command that was failing and now passes. A check that passes the first time is not counted here.
Remember the check's state: passing removes it from failing, failing adds it.
Or a TodoWrite item turned completed, or a file or symbol read for the first time.
Look at the last 6 events.
Count this error signature.
rememberFile (not shown) stores the file hash and says if it matches an earlier one.
The key is tool + input hash + output hash. Three equal keys: same command, same result.
The same error signature three times, even from different commands.
An edit brought a file back to an earlier state: undo and redo.
keys(0) collects the keys at even positions, keys(1) at odd positions.
Six events, one key at even positions and one at odd: A-B-A-B-A-B, ping-pong.
No loop seen.

callout.text: In this order, an exact A-B-A-B-A-B also has 3 equal keys, so line 11 answers first with "same command, same result". The lab's last task shows it. Raise it with the G3-32 owner: check ping-pong before line 11.

sections.h: Routing, part 1: model and effort per job
p: Effort is how hard the model thinks before it answers: low, medium, high or xhigh. In Anthropic's tests, Opus 5.5 at medium, re-running only failed attempts at high, was cheaper and better than high for everything. So the routing table starts most jobs at medium.
The plan (G4) names the job for each step, and the harness looks it up. Helpers are subagents (AgentDefinitions) with their own model and effort.
sections.because: We keep the table in code, because G1's effort sweep will change rows, and a change should be one reviewed line.

notes.text: The four effort levels we use.
A route is a model and an effort.
Readiness checks are short: Sonnet 5.5 at low.
Plans at medium; the plan itself asks for high on fuzzy or cross-module tickets.
build is the fallback for any job not listed.
Helpers read and search with Haiku 5.5 and return file:line pointers.
CI fixers start at low, because CI checks their work. A failure re-runs at medium.
The order in which effort goes up.
64K output tokens. At 16K most long attempts were cut off. Big steps may go up to 128000.
Keep the prompt cache 1 hour for Nova and bug fixers, which wait on people; 5 minutes for routines.

sections.h: Routing, part 2: one level up on failure
p: When a step's checks fail, the harness re-runs that step once, one effort level higher. It does not restart the session. It changes the effort on the running query, so the prompt cache stays warm.
sections.because: We change effort inside the same session, because a restart would throw away the cached context and cost more.

notes.text: Look up a job's route. Unknown jobs fall back to build.
Re-run a failed step one level higher.
The next level, never past xhigh.
applyFlagSettings changes effort on the running query from the next turn. G4's W6 spike checks that cache reads stay at 80% or more.
The session uses streaming input, so we send the retry prompt into the same session.
Return the new route, so the ladder knows where it stands.
test/no-limits.test.ts fails if the session options ever get maxTurns, maxBudgetUsd or taskBudget.

sections.h: The ladder, part 1: rungs inside the turn
p: When the watcher sees no real progress, the harness steps in one rung at a time. The first two rungs happen inside the turn, through the watcher's hook. A PostToolUse hook can return additionalContext: text the model reads with the tool result.
sections.because: We start with words, because a nudge that names the loop is cheap and often enough.

notes.text: The five rungs, in order. The names are also the metric's rung label.
How many flat tool events before each rung. Starting values, tuned from logged verdicts.
inTurnContext returns the text for rungs 1 and 2, or nothing.
After 6 flat events: rung 1, the nudge.
The nudge names the loop and its evidence, and offers a way out: say what blocks you.
After 9 flat events: rung 2, step back and re-plan.
Otherwise, no extra context.

callout.text: To wire it, the watcher's hook returns a text from inTurnContext instead of {}. The shape is { hookSpecificOutput: { hookEventName: "PostToolUse", additionalContext: text } }.

sections.h: The ladder, part 2: rungs between turns
p: Rungs 3 to 5 happen at a step boundary, in the step loop, after a checkpoint. Rung 3 thinks harder, rung 4 starts a fresh session from the notes, rung 5 asks a person. Any real progress resets the ladder.
sections.because: We climb only while progress stays flat, because each rung costs more than the one before.

notes.text: Real progress: reset to index 2, the first between-turns rung.
The next rung to try, by index in RUNGS.
Past the last rung, or not flat long enough yet: do nothing.
Count the hand-off: ai_agents_watcher_handoffs_total{rung}, for alerts and the weekly run review.
Rung 3: re-run the step one effort level higher (section 5).
Rung 4: save everything first.
Then a new session seeded with notes.md: new context, same branch and notes.
Rung 5: ask_human with what was tried and the evidence.
Move to the next rung for the next time.

callout.text: A review finding that comes back after a fix, with the same fingerprint, goes straight to rung 5. G4 provides the fingerprints.

sections.h: Check-ins and the far cost backstop
p: Time is measured, never limited. When a run passes 2 times its own estimate, Nova posts a short check-in and keeps going. It does it again at 4 and 8 times. Only a Stop from a person ends the run.

The backstop is a cost far above a normal ticket, NOVA_BACKSTOP_USD, later about 3 times the 99th percentile of successful runs. Spend comes from the gateway's GET /v1/runs/{run_id}/spend; the SDK's total_cost_usd is the fallback. For the first 4 weeks it runs in shadow mode: it only counts and logs.
sections.because: We check spend only at step boundaries, because the backstop must never cut a run mid-thought.

notes.text: Shadow mode is the default. Live mode needs 4 weeks of data and a decision in the weekly review.
The far-away number. 200 is a placeholder until real data sets it.
afterStep runs after every step, never inside a turn.
Past 2 times the estimate (then 4, then 8)?
Ask the model for a 3-line check-in: what takes time, and why it is worth it.
Post it in the thread with post_progress.
Double the next check-in point, and keep going.
Ask the gateway for this run's spend. The gateway is the source of truth.
Under the backstop: carry on.
Count it either way: ai_agents_backstop_would_pause_total{mode}.
Shadow mode: log the spend and carry on. Nothing else.
Live mode: checkpoint first, so nothing is lost.
Ask. The harness ends with needs_answer, reason backstop; the workflow posts Continue and Stop; Continue resumes the same session.

callout.text: The per-agent monthly limit and the hold on new runs live in the gateway and the queues (G0, lesson g3-10). Not here.

quiz.q: Why does the watcher measure progress instead of time or turns?

options.text: Counting tool events is cheaper than reading a clock.
options.why: Cost is not the reason; the rule is guide, don't cage.

options.text: A slow but useful run is never punished, and a fast loop is still caught.
options.why: Progress (a check that newly passes, a todo done, a new fact) is what matters.

options.text: Temporal workflows may not read the clock.
options.why: The watcher runs in the harness, not in a workflow. The reason is about agents.

quiz.q: A build step's checks fail at medium effort. What does routing do?

options.text: Restarts the session at high effort with a fresh context.
options.why: A restart throws away the warm cache. The same session continues.

options.text: Switches the step to Sonnet 5.5, which is faster.
options.why: The model stays; only the effort goes one level up.

options.text: Re-runs that step once at high, in the same session, through applyFlagSettings.
options.why: One level up, once, then the watcher decides.

quiz.q: In shadow mode, a run's spend passes NOVA_BACKSTOP_USD. What happens?

options.text: The counter ai_agents_backstop_would_pause_total goes up, the spend is logged, and the run continues.
options.why: Shadow mode only counts and logs for the first 4 weeks.

options.text: The run checkpoints and asks Continue or Stop in the thread.
options.why: That is live mode, after 4 weeks of data and a decision.

options.text: The current turn is cut and the run ends.
options.why: Nothing ever cuts a turn. Even live mode waits for the step boundary.

The number of tool events since the last real progress.
The watcher's name for a loop: same command and result, same error, undo and redo, or ping-pong.
Five steps the harness takes on flat progress: nudge, re-plan, think harder, fresh start, ask a person.
How hard the model thinks before answering: low, medium, high or xhigh.
A cost far above a normal ticket that pauses a run between steps and asks a person.
Running a rule that only counts and logs what it would do, to collect data first.
